To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the relative reproductive effort towards male and female strategies is a function of the relative fitness of the male and female reproductive strategies, and that in wind-pollination, the male strategy is less fit than the female strategy.
the relative investment in male and female reproductive effort in wind-pollination species is a function of the degree of self-incompatibility and the relative costs of male and female reproduction.

1) in self-compatible, wind-pollinated, monoecious species, the majority of the total reproductive energy goes to seed production; 2) self-incompatible, wind-pollination species, on the other hand, invest about equally in pollen and ovule production; and 3) the method described here can be used to quantify male and female effort for both wind and insect pollination.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of reproductive effort in plants and the relative allocation of this effort to the male, female, and vegetative components of the reproductive strategy.
the evolution of the male and female reproductive strategies in flowering plants.
the evolution of sex allocation in plants, with a special interest in wind-pollination.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relative effort of the two reproductive strategies is dependent on both the genetic and the environmental factors.
in wind-pollinating species, the female effort is generally greater than male effort.
in wind-pollination, the female sex is the major reproductive effort, and the male effort represents the minor reproductive effort.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in wind-pollination, the male strategy has been reduced in relative effort to the female strategy.

the relative reproductive effort to the sexes in wind-pollination is a function of the self-incompatibility system of the plant, and that the relative reproductive efforts of the sexes are not a function of whether the plant has insect- or wind-pollination.
the reproductive effort in the male sex of wind-pollinated plant species is generally much smaller, relative to the female effort, than in insect-pollinated plant populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in wind-pollination, the female effort is the main reproductive effort.
, for wind-pollinated monoecious species, female effort represents the bulk of the reproductive effort in these species.

, in wind-pollination, female reproductive effort is usually much higher than male effort, and the ratio of female effort to male effort is a good measure of the degree of self-compatibility of a wind-pollinated plant.
